senses.gloss: Weak, or without the nerve to do something — said with mild contempt.
examples: Don't be *wimpy* — just tell her what you think.
He made some *wimpy* excuse and left early.
The coffee here is *wimpier* than the stuff at the diner.

senses.gloss: Messy or bent out of shape by the wind.
examples: She came in with *windblown* hair and red cheeks.
The pines along the cliff are low and *windblown*.
His *windblown* look takes twenty minutes in front of the mirror.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *I was winded*
contrast: *Winded* (out of breath) is /ˈwɪndɪd/. The verb *wind* meaning to turn is /waɪnd/, and its participle *wound* /waʊnd/ is a different word again.

senses.gloss: Out of breath after effort or a blow.
examples: I was completely *winded* after the third flight of stairs.
He gets *winded* just carrying the groceries in.
The tackle left her *winded* but not hurt.

contrast: Say /ˈwaɪndɪŋ/, with the vowel of *find*. The weather word *windy* is /ˈwɪndi/.

senses.gloss: Turning first one way and then the other instead of running straight.
examples: We took a *winding* road through the hills.
A long, *winding* staircase led up to the tower.
The path is narrow and *winding*, so drive slowly.

senses.gloss: Open to the wind, with nothing to block it.
examples: They got married on a *windswept* beach in Maine.
The *windswept* plains go on for hundreds of miles.
It is a beautiful house, but the yard is cold and *windswept*.

senses.gloss: Blown out of place by the wind.
examples: She pushed her *windswept* hair out of her face.
He showed up half an hour late and thoroughly *windswept*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a windup toy*
form: compound — from the phrasal verb *wind up*
contrast: Also written *wind-up*. The noun *windup* is the pitcher's motion in baseball.

senses.gloss: Worked by a spring that you turn with a key or a handle.
examples: The baby loves that little *windup* penguin.
He collects old *windup* clocks.
It is a *windup* flashlight, so you never need batteries.

senses.gloss: With a lot of wind blowing.
examples: It is cold and *windy* out there — take a jacket.
Chicago is *windier* than people expect in the spring.
We picked the *windiest* day of the year to go sailing.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a winged insect*
contrast: In poetry and in a few fixed phrases it has two syllables: /ˈwɪŋɪd/.

senses.gloss: Having wings.
examples: Ants produce *winged* forms once a year.
A *winged* statue stands over the entrance.
*Winged* seeds spin down from the maple in May.

senses.gloss: Without a single win.
senses.ru: без побед, не выигравший ни разу
examples: The team is still *winless* after nine games.
They ended a *winless* season by firing the coach.
He is *winless* in his last twelve starts.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the winning goal*
comparison: more/most — *more winning*, *most winning* — only in the 'charming' sense
contrast: Before a noun it is an adjective; in *we are winning* it is part of the verb.

senses.gloss: That wins, or that has won.
examples: She scored the *winning* goal in the last minute.
Here are tonight's *winning* numbers.
The *winning* team goes to the finals.

senses.gloss: Charming in a way that makes people like you right away.
examples: He has a *winning* smile and he knows it.
Her *winning* manner got them through the door.

form: -some — from an old word for joy, not from *win*
contrast: Slightly literary. *Charming* or *appealing* is the everyday word.

senses.gloss: Attractive in a simple, cheerful way.
examples: A *winsome* kid with a gap-toothed grin answered the door.
The movie has a *winsome* lead and not much else.
She was *winsome* on camera and tough in the meeting.

senses.gloss: Cold and gray, the way winter is.
examples: A *wintry* mix of rain and snow is on the way.
It felt *wintrier* than usual for early October.
We drove home under a low, *wintry* sky.

senses.gloss: Cold and unfriendly.
examples: She gave him a *wintry* smile and kept walking.
His answer was polite but *wintry*.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *I'm wiped out*
form: compound — from the phrasal verb *wipe out*
contrast: The same words serve as the passive of the verb (*the storm wiped out the crop*); the adjective is the 'exhausted' one, and it never goes before a noun.

senses.gloss: Completely exhausted.
examples: I'm *wiped out* — I'm going to bed.
The kids were *wiped out* after the water park.
She sounded *wiped out* on the phone.

senses.gloss: Too keyed up to settle down, often from caffeine.
examples: Three cups of coffee and I'm totally *wired*.
The kids are *wired* from all that sugar.
He was still *wired* an hour after the game.

senses.gloss: Fitted with wiring, or connected to a network.
examples: Every room in the building is *wired* for internet.
The house was *wired* in 1954 and needs an update.

senses.gloss: Working without a cable.
examples: We finally got a *wireless* printer.
The keyboard is *wireless*, so there is no cable to trip over.
Ask the front desk for the *wireless* password.

senses.gloss: Thin but strong.
examples: He is *wiry* — all muscle and no weight.
A *wiry* little terrier came running down the hall.
The climbers were *wirier* than any of us expected.

senses.gloss: Stiff and springy, like wire.
examples: She has thick, *wiry* hair.
The dog has a *wiry* coat that never lies flat.

position: attributive only — almost always in *wishful thinking*
contrast: Practically a one-phrase word: *wishful thinking*. You cannot say *I was wishful*.

senses.gloss: Based on what you hope for rather than on the facts.
examples: Saying the deal will close by Friday is *wishful* thinking.
That is a nice plan, but it is mostly *wishful* thinking.
A little *wishful* thinking never hurt anybody.

form: compound — a rhyming double of *washy*, watered down

senses.gloss: Weak and undecided, without a clear position.
examples: He gave a *wishy-washy* answer that satisfied nobody.
Don't be so *wishy-washy* — pick a restaurant.
The report's conclusion is *wishy-washy* on purpose.

senses.gloss: Thin, light and not thick enough to hold together.
examples: *Wispy* clouds hung over the lake.
He has a *wispy* little beard.
Her hair is finer and *wispier* than it used to be.

senses.gloss: Quietly sad about something you miss or cannot have.
examples: She sounded *wistful* about her old neighborhood.
He gave the house one last, *wistful* look.
There is a *wistful* tone to the whole album.

senses.gloss: Quiet and closed off, not wanting to be with people.
examples: He has been quiet and *withdrawn* since the move.
She became more *withdrawn* after her sister left.
Teachers noticed a *withdrawn*, silent kid in the back row.

senses.gloss: Dried up and shrunken from age or lack of water.
examples: The plants on the porch were brown and *withered*.
A few *withered* apples still hung on the tree.
His *withered* left hand never fully recovered.

contrast: Here it means crushing, not drying up. The plant meaning stays with the verb: *the flowers are withering*.

senses.gloss: So scornful or harsh that it crushes the person it is aimed at.
examples: She shot him a *withering* look across the table.
The senator faced *withering* criticism from her own party.
His response was brief and *withering*.

senses.gloss: Funny in a quick, clever way.
examples: She is the *wittiest* person in the room, every time.
He wrote a short, *witty* thank-you note.
The dialogue is *witty* without trying too hard.

contrast: Two syllables: /ˈwɪzənd/, with the vowel of *wizard*.

senses.gloss: Small, dry and lined with age.
examples: A *wizened* old man sold tickets at the door.
Her hands were small and *wizened*.
*Wizened* apples sat in a bowl by the window.

senses.gloss: Moving from side to side instead of staying steady.
examples: This table is *wobbly* — put something under the leg.
My legs felt *wobbly* after the flu.
The back wheel got *wobblier* with every mile.

senses.gloss: Bad enough to be embarrassing.
examples: The team's defense was *woeful* all season.
There is a *woeful* lack of parking downtown.
His Spanish is *woeful*, but he keeps trying.

senses.gloss: Full of sadness.
examples: She told the whole *woeful* story over coffee.
The dog gave me a *woeful* look from the doorway.

form: -ly from *woman* — an adjective, not an adverb
contrast: An *-ly* word that is an adjective: *a womanly figure*, never *she smiled womanly*. Compare *womanish*, which is an insult.

senses.gloss: Having the qualities or the shape thought of as a grown woman's.
examples: She had a calm, *womanly* authority in the room.
The dress was cut to show a *womanly* shape.
He praised what he called her *womanly* patience — she was not flattered.

contrast: Already a strong word, so *very wonderful* sounds odd; say *absolutely wonderful*.

senses.gloss: Extremely good or pleasant.
examples: We had a *wonderful* time in Vermont.
That smells *wonderful* — what is it?
She has been absolutely *wonderful* about the whole thing.

contrast: Literary or half-joking in modern American English; *wonderful* or *amazing* is the everyday word.

senses.gloss: Strange and beautiful enough to make you wonder at it.
examples: The canyon at sunrise is a *wondrous* sight.
He told *wondrous* stories about his years at sea.
The exhibit is full of *wondrous* little machines.

form: -y — the policy sense is from *wonk*, a detail-obsessed expert

senses.gloss: Crooked, shaky or not working right — informal.
examples: The shelf is a little *wonky* on the left.
My knee has been *wonky* since the hike.
The app gets *wonkier* with every update.

senses.gloss: Full of technical detail, the way a policy expert talks.
examples: It is a *wonky* piece about tax credits.
The conversation got *wonky* fast.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a wood-burning stove*

senses.gloss: Burning wood as fuel.
examples: They put a *wood-burning* stove in the cabin.
The house has a *wood-burning* fireplace.
*Wood-burning* heaters are banned on high-pollution days.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a wood-fired oven*

senses.gloss: Heated by a wood fire, said of ovens, grills and what comes out of them.
examples: They bake everything in a *wood-fired* oven.
We split a *wood-fired* pizza and a salad.
The restaurant's *wood-fired* grill runs all day.

senses.gloss: Covered with trees.
examples: The trail runs through a *wooded* valley.
They bought a *wooded* lot outside of town.
The north side of the island is more heavily *wooded*.

senses.gloss: Like wood in smell, taste or texture.
examples: The wine has a *woody* finish.
Older asparagus goes *woody* at the bottom.
The candle has a warm, *woody* smell.

senses.gloss: Covered with trees.
examples: A *woody* hillside rises behind the house.
We camped in a *woodier* part of the park.

contrast: *Woolly* keeps both *l*'s, but the related adjective is *woolen* in American English and *woollen* in British.

senses.gloss: Made of wool, or thick and soft like wool.
examples: He pulled on a *woolly* hat and gloves.
The puppy still has its *woolly* undercoat.
That old blanket is the *woolliest* thing in the house.

senses.gloss: Vague and badly organized, of thinking or writing.
examples: The argument goes *woolly* in the middle.
That is *woolly* thinking, not a plan.

senses.gloss: Dizzy and slightly sick.
senses.ru: с головокружением, мутный, дурно себя чувствующий
examples: I felt *woozy* when I stood up too fast.
The medication made her *woozy* for an hour.
He got *woozier* as the heat went up.

ru: из уст в уста, по сарафанному радио
position: attributive only — before a noun: *word-of-mouth advertising*
form: compound — from the phrase *by word of mouth*
contrast: Hyphens before a noun. After a verb use the noun phrase instead: *the restaurant grew by word of mouth*.

senses.gloss: Spread by people telling each other rather than by advertising.
senses.ru: передающийся из уст в уста, сарафанный
examples: The band built its audience on *word-of-mouth* buzz.
*Word-of-mouth* recommendations beat every ad we ran.
It was a *word-of-mouth* hit before the reviews came out.

senses.gloss: Without any words spoken.
examples: They exchanged a *wordless* look and got up.
The film ends with a long, *wordless* scene.
He answered with a *wordless* shrug.

senses.gloss: Using more words than it needs.
examples: The contract is *wordy* and hard to follow.
Your introduction is *wordier* than it needs to be.
Cut the *wordiest* paragraphs first.

senses.gloss: Good enough to be put into practice.
examples: We finally have a *workable* plan.
Is that schedule *workable* for you?
It is not perfect, but it is *workable*.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *don't get worked up*
form: compound — from the phrasal verb *work up*

senses.gloss: Upset or excited about something, usually more than it deserves.
examples: Don't get *worked up* about something that has not happened.
He was all *worked up* over a parking ticket.
She gets *worked up* before every presentation.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a working mother*
contrast: Only before a noun. After a verb, *is working* is the verb: *the elevator is working again*.

senses.gloss: Having a paid job.
examples: Day care is expensive for *working* parents.
Most of our students are *working* adults.
She has been a *working* musician since she was nineteen.

senses.gloss: In operation, not broken.
examples: Is there a *working* bathroom on this floor?
The museum has a *working* model of the mill.
We need a *working* phone number for the file.

senses.gloss: Good enough to go on with for now.
examples: I have a *working* knowledge of Spanish.
The *working* title was 'The Long Way Home.'
That is our *working* assumption until we hear otherwise.

form: compound — the noun phrase *working class* used as an adjective
contrast: Hyphenated as an adjective (*a working-class neighborhood*); the noun phrase is two words (*the working class*).

senses.gloss: Belonging to the part of society that does manual or hourly work.
examples: He grew up in a *working-class* neighborhood in Cleveland.
Her family is *working-class* and proud of it.
The movie is about *working-class* kids in the 1970s.

senses.gloss: As good as the best anywhere in the world.
examples: The hospital has a *world-class* cancer center.
She is a *world-class* cellist.
The food is good, but it is not *world-class*.

senses.gloss: Tired of life, having seen too much of it to be surprised by anything.
examples: He plays a *world-weary* detective with a bad knee.
She sounded *world-weary* for someone of twenty-five.
There is a *world-weary* humor running through his writing.

contrast: The same word is also an adverb: *the book sold two million copies worldwide*.

senses.gloss: Happening or existing everywhere in the world.
examples: The company has *worldwide* distribution.
It became a *worldwide* phenomenon overnight.
Demand is *worldwide*, not just here.

senses.gloss: Damaged or made thin by long use.
examples: The carpet is *worn* in front of the door.
He wore a *worn* leather jacket and no hat.
These tires are more *worn* than they look.

senses.gloss: Looking tired and used up.
examples: Her face looked *worn* after the night shift.
He seemed thin and *worn* when we saw him in May.

form: compound — from the phrasal verb *wear out*
contrast: Hyphen before a noun (*worn-out shoes*); after a verb most Americans write it as two words: *I'm worn out*.

senses.gloss: Too old or damaged to be used any longer.
examples: He finally threw out his *worn-out* sneakers.
A *worn-out* couch sat by the curb all week.
The engine parts are *worn out* and need replacing.

senses.gloss: Completely exhausted.
examples: I'm *worn out* from the drive.
The nurses are *worn out* and short-staffed.

contrast: Americans say *worrisome*; the British usually say *worrying*.

senses.gloss: Giving you reason to worry.
examples: The test results are *worrisome* but not conclusive.
There is a *worrisome* crack in the ceiling.
The most *worrisome* part is how fast it spread.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *worsening weather*

senses.gloss: Getting worse as time goes on.
examples: *Worsening* weather forced them to turn back.
Doctors pointed to his *worsening* symptoms.
The report describes a *worsening* housing shortage.

senses.gloss: Having no value at all.
examples: The stock turned out to be *worthless*.
Without the receipt the warranty is *worthless*.
He inherited a box of *worthless* old bonds.

senses.gloss: Good for nothing — of a person.
examples: Depression can make you feel *worthless*.
His father called him *worthless* one too many times.

contrast: *Worthwhile* is one word and needs no preposition. *Worth* takes a noun or *-ing* straight after it: *worth the money*, *worth doing*.

senses.gloss: Worth the time, money or trouble it costs.
examples: It is a long drive, but the museum is *worthwhile*.
We made a few *worthwhile* changes to the draft.
It is *worthwhile* to call ahead and check.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a would-be writer*
contrast: It marks someone trying or hoping to be something, usually with a hint that they have not managed it: *a would-be actor* has not made it yet.

senses.gloss: Hoping or trying to be the thing named.
examples: The city is full of *would-be* screenwriters.
A *would-be* thief got stuck in the window.
She gives advice to *would-be* founders.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *he was wound up*
form: compound — from the phrasal verb *wind up*
contrast: Here *wound* rhymes with *found*. The noun *wound* (an injury) is /wuːnd/ and is a different word.

senses.gloss: Tense and excited, unable to relax.
examples: He was too *wound up* to sleep.
She gets *wound up* about deadlines.
The kids are all *wound up* tonight.

senses.gloss: Made by crossing threads or strips over and under each other.
examples: A *woven* basket sat by the fireplace.
The chair has a *woven* cane seat.
She brought back a hand-*woven* rug from Oaxaca.

contrast: Sounds exactly like *rapt*, which means completely absorbed: *a rapt audience*.

senses.gloss: Covered in paper, cloth or plastic.
examples: The sandwiches are *wrapped* and in the fridge.
She handed me a small, *wrapped* box.
The statue stayed *wrapped* in plastic all winter.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *she's wrapped up in work*
form: compound — from the phrasal verb *wrap up*

senses.gloss: So absorbed in something that you notice nothing else.
examples: He is completely *wrapped up* in his own problems.
She was so *wrapped up* in the book that she missed her stop.
They are too *wrapped up* in each other to notice.

senses.gloss: Finished and settled.
examples: Everything is *wrapped up* — we can go home.
With the paperwork *wrapped up*, we finally relaxed.

senses.gloss: Badly damaged or destroyed.
examples: A *wrecked* car sat in the driveway for months.
They photographed the *wrecked* buildings from the air.
Divers found the *wrecked* fishing boat in forty feet of water.

senses.gloss: Completely exhausted — informal.
examples: I was *wrecked* after the red-eye.
She is *wrecked* by the time the kids go to bed.

senses.gloss: Causing sharp emotional pain.
examples: It was a *wrenching* decision to sell the farm.
The last chapter is *wrenching*.
They made a *wrenching* documentary about the flood.

contrast: The *-ed* is a full syllable: /ˈrɛtʃɪd/, like *naked* and *wicked*.

senses.gloss: Very unhappy, or living in miserable conditions.
examples: He felt *wretched* about the way he had spoken to her.
The families lived in *wretched* conditions all winter.
I had the flu and felt absolutely *wretched*.

senses.gloss: Very bad in quality.
examples: The service was *wretched* and the food was worse.
We sat through a *wretched* second half.

senses.gloss: Full of creases, of cloth or paper.
examples: His shirt was *wrinkled* from the suitcase.
She smoothed out a *wrinkled* receipt on the counter.
Linen looks *wrinkled* no matter what you do.

senses.gloss: Lined with age, of skin.
examples: His hands were brown and *wrinkled*.
A *wrinkled* face broke into a grin.

contrast: *Wrinkly* describes how something looks; *wrinkled* says what happened to it.

senses.gloss: Covered in small folds or creases.
examples: The puppy has *wrinkly* little legs.
My fingers got *wrinkly* in the bath.
This shirt is even *wrinklier* than the last one.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *written permission*
contrast: Only before a noun in this sense. After a verb, *is written* is the verb: *the rule is written down somewhere*.

senses.gloss: Put down in writing rather than spoken.
examples: You need *written* permission from a parent.
There is a *written* test and a road test.
Their *written* English is better than their speaking.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *wrongful termination*
contrast: A legal word: *wrongful death*, *wrongful termination*, *wrongful conviction*. For everyday wrongness use *wrong*.

senses.gloss: Done unfairly or against the law.
examples: She sued the company for *wrongful* termination.
The family filed a *wrongful* death claim.
He spent nine years in prison after a *wrongful* conviction.

contrast: Also written *wrong-headed*. It attacks the thinking behind a decision, not just the result.

senses.gloss: Based on stubbornly bad judgment.
examples: The whole policy is *wrongheaded*.
That is a *wrongheaded* way to read the data.
Cutting the budget now would be *wrongheaded*.

senses.gloss: Dryly funny about something that is not really funny.
examples: He has a *wry* sense of humor about getting older.
Her *wry* commentary is the best part of the show.
The book is sad and *wry* at the same time.

senses.gloss: Twisted a little to one side, showing amusement or distaste.
examples: She gave a *wry* smile and shook her head.
He made a *wry* face at the first sip.

senses.gloss: Hostile toward foreigners.
examples: The party's platform got more *xenophobic* every year.
He apologized for a *xenophobic* remark.
The campaign ran an openly *xenophobic* ad.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *Yankee ingenuity*
contrast: Inside the US it means a New Englander or a Northerner; outside it means any American. Always capitalized, and most often a noun (*a Yankee*).

senses.gloss: Of the northern United States, especially New England.
examples: He liked to talk about *Yankee* ingenuity.
She kept the *Yankee* habit of saving everything.
The book follows *Yankee* traders across the Pacific.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a yawning gap*
contrast: In this sense it means wide open, not sleepy. *A yawning student* is simply one who is yawning.

senses.gloss: Wide open, of a gap, a hole or a difference.
examples: There is a *yawning* gap between the two offers.
A *yawning* hole opened in the street.
The report points to a *yawning* skills shortage.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the year-end report*

senses.gloss: Happening at or covering the end of the year.
examples: The *year-end* report goes out in January.
She got a nice *year-end* bonus.
*Year-end* sales cleared out the old stock.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a year-round school*
contrast: The same word is an adverb after the verb: *the pool is open year-round*.

senses.gloss: Going on through all four seasons.
examples: The district moved to a *year-round* school calendar.
It is a *year-round* resort, not just a ski town.
They need *year-round* staff, not seasonal help.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a yearlong study*

senses.gloss: Lasting a whole year.
examples: She is on a *yearlong* leave from the university.
The museum is closing for a *yearlong* renovation.
It was a *yearlong* study of four hundred families.

form: from the verb *yellow* — turned yellow with age

senses.gloss: Turned yellow with age.
examples: He kept a box of *yellowed* newspaper clippings.
The pages are *yellowed* and brittle.
*Yellowed* lace curtains hung in the front window.

senses.gloss: Slightly yellow.
examples: The walls are a *yellowish* white.
The light in the hallway is *yellowish* and dim.
It leaves a *yellowish* stain on the fabric.

contrast: Also a noun for the person: *a Yemeni*, *two Yemenis*. Always capitalized.

senses.gloss: From Yemen, or having to do with Yemen.
examples: We ate at a *Yemeni* restaurant in Dearborn.
*Yemeni* coffee is famous.
Her husband is *Yemeni*.

contrast: *Youthful* means young-seeming or typical of young people; *young* is the plain fact of age. A sixty-year-old can look *youthful* but is not *young*.

senses.gloss: Young in the way you look or act, or belonging to a person's young years.
examples: She has a *youthful* energy that wears the rest of us out.
He apologized for his *youthful* mistakes.
At seventy he still looks *youthful*.

contrast: A child's word — fine at the kitchen table, out of place in writing.

senses.gloss: Disgusting, especially to taste or touch.
examples: There is something *yucky* in the bottom of the sink.
The medicine tastes *yucky*.
This is the *yuckiest* one in the whole box.

contrast: Historical: Yugoslavia broke up in the 1990s. For today's countries say *Serbian*, *Croatian*, *Bosnian* or *Slovenian*. *Yugoslavian* is the other adjective form.

senses.gloss: From the former Yugoslavia, or having to do with it.
examples: His parents came over on a *Yugoslav* passport.
The museum has a room of *Yugoslav* film posters.
She studies the *Yugoslav* economy of the 1970s.

contrast: Casual and a little childlike; in writing use *delicious*.

senses.gloss: Very good to eat.
examples: Something *yummy* is coming out of the oven.
These are even *yummier* with chocolate chips.
The soup was *yummy*, thanks.

contrast: Also a noun for the person: *a Zambian*. Always capitalized.

senses.gloss: From Zambia, or having to do with Zambia.
examples: The *Zambian* team qualified for the final.
He teaches *Zambian* history.
Her mother is *Zambian*.

senses.gloss: Funny in a silly, unpredictable way.
examples: It is a *zany* comedy about a family road trip.
He has a *zany* sense of humor.
Each sketch is *zanier* than the last.

contrast: Note the vowel: /ˈzɛləs/, even though *zeal* is /ziːl/.

senses.gloss: Working for something with great, sometimes excessive energy.
examples: He is *zealous* about recycling.
*Zealous* fans camped out overnight for tickets.
The most *zealous* reformers went too far.

senses.gloss: Sharp and lively in flavor, or full of energy.
examples: The dressing is light and *zesty*.
Add lime to make the salsa *zestier*.
It is a *zesty* little tune for the opening credits.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a zigzag pattern*
contrast: Also a verb (*the trail zigzags up the hill*) and a noun. As an adjective it only goes before a noun.

senses.gloss: Made of short sharp turns, first one way and then the other.
examples: The sweater has a *zigzag* pattern across the chest.
A *zigzag* path leads down to the water.
He drew a *zigzag* line under the title.

contrast: Also a noun for the person: *a Zimbabwean*. Always capitalized.

senses.gloss: From Zimbabwe, or having to do with Zimbabwe.
examples: The *Zimbabwean* dollar collapsed in 2008.
He is a *Zimbabwean* novelist living in Texas.
Two of the players are *Zimbabwean*.

contrast: Capitalized. It names support for a Jewish state in Israel, and it is a political label that some speakers use as an insult, so the speaker matters.

senses.gloss: Supporting a Jewish national state in Israel, or having to do with that movement.
examples: The book covers the early *Zionist* movement in Europe.
He writes from an openly *Zionist* point of view.
*Zionist* and anti-*Zionist* groups held rival rallies.

senses.gloss: Fast and lively.
examples: It is a *zippy* little car for city driving.
The new laptop is *zippier* than my old one.
She gave a *zippy* two-minute summary.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a zoological survey*
contrast: Watch the first syllables: /ˌzoʊə-/, two syllables, not the /zuː/ of *zoo*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the scientific study of animals.
examples: The *zoological* garden opened in 1891.
She published a *zoological* survey of the island.
It is a *zoological* term, not an everyday one.

form: from *zoonosis*, a disease that passes from animals to people

senses.gloss: Of a disease that spreads from animals to people.
examples: Rabies is a *zoonotic* disease.
Most new epidemics are *zoonotic* in origin.
They study *zoonotic* spillover in bat populations.
